title: Cost & Economies of Scale

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the sources of cost advantage

Know and understand the following economic concepts and how they relate to one another: fixed costs, variable costs, total cost, average fixed cost, average variable cost, average total cost, marginal cost, economies of scale
Understand the strategic implications of economies of scale (i.e., when does it make sense to grow?)

keyTerms.def: Defines the relationship between production (Q) and total cost (C). Total cost can be broken into fixed (FC) and variable costs (VC).
The part of the cost function that does not change with Q (the constant term).
keyTerms.src: S06 Video Slides p.14; CQ3 Q1 feedback

keyTerms.def: Every term that changes with Q.
keyTerms.src: S06 Video Slides p.15; CQ3 Q2 feedback

keyTerms.def: The cost of producing an additional unit of output, or the change in cost attributable to the last unit of output. MC = ΔC/ΔQ = dC/dQ.
In the short run, capital (e.g., number of grills) is fixed and labor is variable; in the long run a manager is free to adjust all inputs — all costs are variable.
Defines the minimum average cost of producing alternative levels of output, allowing for optimal selection of fixed and variable factors of production.
Exist when long-run average costs decline as output is increased.
Exist when long-run average costs rise as output is increased.
'Practice makes perfect': firms become more efficient through practice; costs fall with cumulative output over time, whereas economies of scale come from the volume produced in a given period.
Cost per unit (y) plotted against scale (x), fit with a power function y = a·x^b. Slope of the curve = 2^b = cost multiplier per doubling; % drop per doubling = 1 − 2^b.
keyTerms.src: S06 workbook Solution!B49-E84; Cost Advantage Part 1 step 5

cases: Competing on cost (S06 slides p.7): Kroger competes on cost (keeps 21¢ of each sales dollar after groceries vs. Whole Foods 36¢); Whole Foods on differentiation (premium covers overhead of 29% vs. Kroger's 18%); Kroger wins on volume ($3.50 sales per $ assets vs. $2.50); Safeway is stuck in the middle (1.5% operating margin; Albertsons bought it a year later); most successful in 2014: Whole Foods — best margins and ROA; Kroger's higher ROE comes mostly from debt.

HSIA Wars: Guest-Tek offered HSIA at $0.10 per room per day (early 2007); iBahn earned ~$0.65 on fixed-fee contracts; iBahn ~200,000 rooms, Guest-Tek ~500,000 after GoldenTree; ~2.5M rooms excluding 5-star; iBahn differentiated on security/VPN and 7-minute support calls (HSIA Wars case pp.1-3)

Guest-Tek verdict: can afford $0.10 since MC at current volume ≈ $0.10; but to cover fixed costs at that price they'd need ~2.2M rooms ≈ 88% of 2.5M select-service rooms; the competitor had a quality differentiator and scope economies, so Guest-Tek risked a price war it couldn't win (S06 workbook Solution!A112-A153)

Netflix vs. Redbox (Cost Advantage assignment): Redbox ATC per rental = 656.06·R^−0.476 (TC = 656.06·R^0.524); Netflix CPSPM = 38.10·S^−0.182; Redbox cost falls ~28.1% per doubling vs. Netflix ~11.9%; Netflix MCPEH ≈ $0.096/hr vs. Redbox ≈ $0.65/hr in 2016-2 (Kimball's Cost Advantage workbook — his answers, not an official key)
'Scale economies work in reverse': Redbox's rentals were shrinking, moving it UP its steep scale curve (Kimball's Cost Advantage Part 1 step 6)
traps: MC excludes fixed costs (marginal cost is only the variable cost of the last unit)
MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimum points
ATC − AVC = AFC, which shrinks toward zero as Q rises
Units: Guest-Tek costs are in $000s; convert rooms to room-days (×365/4)
Learning/experience = cumulative output over time; scale = volume in a period
Video slide p.16 prints 'C = 8 + 58 = $58' — the correct arithmetic is 8 + 50 = $58
